The Ming Dynasty. From 1368 to 1644 CE, the Ming was a restoration of Han Chinese rule after the Mongol Yuan Dynasty, lasting nearly three hundred years and producing some of the world's most iconic architecture and art. Founded by Zhu Yuanzhang, Emperor Hongwu, a former peasant who rose through military skill and ruthlessness, the Ming reasserted Confucian governance and Han cultural pride. The dynasty is celebrated for constructing the Forbidden City in Beijing, the Great Wall in its modern form, and dispatching the treasure voyages of Admiral Zheng He, which reached Africa nearly a century before European explorers. Ming blue-and-white porcelain, landscape painting, and literature defined the aesthetic of the era. However, the dynasty's later emperors became increasingly isolated; the empire turned inward, ceding global maritime dominance to European powers, and eventually succumbed to Manchu invasion in 1644 CE.

Zhu Yuanzhang, Emperor Hongwu, reigned from 1368 to 1398 CE. A peasant-turned-military-commander, he overthrew the Yuan and restored Han rule. He executed brutal consolidation: purged potential rivals, executed thousands, and created a surveillance state with secret police called the Jinyiwei to suppress dissent. He established the capital at Nanjing initially, later moved to Beijing by his son Yongle, who reigned from 1402 to 1424 CE.

Emperor Yongle rebuilt Beijing and commissioned the Forbidden City from 1406 to 1420 CE, the imperial palace complex of unparalleled scale and architectural refinement. The Forbidden City housed the imperial court, concubines, bureaucrats, and thousands of servants and was forbidden to commoners. Beijing became the dynasty's cultural and political heart; the city expanded into a metropolis of over one million.

Admiral Zheng He, who lived from 1371 to 1433 CE, was a Muslim eunuch and military commander who led seven massive treasure voyages from 1405 to 1433 CE. Zheng He's fleets, some sources claim over three hundred ships crewed by twenty-eight thousand sailors, sailed to Southeast Asia, India, East Africa, and possibly beyond. The voyages were diplomatic and commercial, displaying Ming power and establishing tributary relationships; they did not establish colonies. They brought exotic animals like giraffes, goods, and knowledge back to China, demonstrating Chinese maritime and navigational superiority.

The Ming rebuilt and reinforced the Great Wall, creating the iconic structure visible today, thousands of miles of brick and stone fortifications against Mongol invasion. They erected grand temples, pagodas, and government buildings; architecture showcased innovation in scale, precision, and aesthetic refinement.

Ming porcelain, especially blue-and-white ceramics, became globally prized and exported worldwide. The Ming perfected glazing, kilning, and decorative techniques; Ming porcelain defined global luxury ceramics for centuries. They applied the same refinement to lacquerware, silk textiles, and furniture.

Ming drama called chuanqi evolved from Yuan traditions; playwrights like Tang Xianzu created psychologically complex, emotionally rich works. Ming poetry and prose fiction flourished; Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Journey to the West, though not entirely Ming compositions, were finalized during this era. Court culture emphasized refined aesthetics: literati painting, calligraphy, poetry, and philosophical discussion.

The Ming restored the civil-service examination system; Han scholars filled the bureaucracy with Confucian ideology. They promoted Neo-Confucianism as orthodox state philosophy and suppressed other intellectual traditions. Over time, Confucian conservatism stifled innovation; the imperial examination became rote memorization of Zhu Xi's commentaries.

After Zheng He's voyages ended in 1433 CE, the Ming court retreated from maritime exploration and global trade. They ceded naval dominance to European powers, who were just beginning to expand globally. Internal strife, particularly between eunuchs and literati bureaucrats, destabilized governance. Economic strain, peasant rebellions, and Jurchen pressure from the north weakened the dynasty.

Li Zicheng led a peasant rebellion that sacked Beijing in 1644 CE; the last Ming emperor hanged himself. The Manchus, from Jurchen stock, invaded from the north and quickly conquered China, establishing the Qing Dynasty.

The Ming Dynasty represented both the zenith and the beginning of the decline of traditional Chinese civilization's global position. The Forbidden City, the Great Wall, and Zheng He's voyages epitomized Ming ambition and capability. Yet the Ming's decision to abandon maritime exploration proved catastrophic. Within a century, European explorers would circumnavigate the globe and establish global trade networks. The Ming failed to recognize this shift; by 1600 CE, China had become isolated. The dynasty's fall to the Manchus ushered in the final imperial dynasty, the Qing, which would oversee China's encounter with Western imperial power.
